faq.q: Is a phone under ₹25,000 good enough for gaming?
faq.a: Yes. Snapdragon 7s Gen 2, Dimensity 8200 and Dimensity 8300-class chipsets handle BGMI and Genshin at medium-to-high settings. Pair with a phone that has a 120Hz AMOLED and a vapour-chamber cooling system for sustained performance.

faq.q: Should I get AMOLED or LCD in this range?
faq.a: AMOLED is the default at ₹25,000 now. You get true blacks, better outdoor visibility on 1,800+ nit panels, and lower battery drain when using dark mode. LCD only makes sense if you specifically want the cheapest possible phone.
8GB is the practical minimum in 2026, 12GB is comfortable for heavy multitasking and on-device AI. Storage: 128GB is the floor, 256GB is worth the ₹1,500–₹2,000 premium if you shoot a lot of video.

faq.q: Are mid-range phones good for photography?
faq.a: Mid-range phones with a 50MP Sony IMX890/IMX882 or Samsung GN8 main sensor and OIS take genuinely good daylight and low-light photos. Telephoto is rare; expect a competent 2MP macro that you will rarely use.

faq.q: How long will software updates last?
faq.a: Samsung offers 4 years of OS + 5 years of security on Galaxy A and M series. OnePlus, Nothing, Motorola and Realme offer 2-3 years of OS updates. If long-term updates matter, Samsung and Pixel A-series are the safer picks.

meta.tldr_pick: Our top pick is the OnePlus Nord CE 4 Lite 5G (current 8/256GB variant). You get a 120Hz AMOLED, 5,500mAh battery, 80W SUPERVOOC charging, and three years of OxygenOS updates. It is the easiest mid-range phone to live with for the next three years.
key_takeaways: AMOLED 120Hz is the new default at ₹25,000 — never settle for LCD at this price.
Snapdragon 7-series or Dimensity 8200+ chipsets handle gaming and AI features without lag.
5,000mAh+ battery with 67W+ fast charging is the practical minimum for heavy users.
OIS on the main camera matters more than a high megapixel count in this range.
meta.who_for: Anyone upgrading from a budget phone under ₹15,000 or replacing a 3-year-old mid-ranger. This list suits people who use their phone heavily for photos, social media, light gaming, and want two-to-three years of updates.
meta.methodology: We compared current 2026 mid-range phones available on Amazon India, Flipkart and brand stores. For each, we evaluated chipset, display, battery, charging, camera, software support, and build. Picks were validated against manufacturer specs, BGR/91mobiles reviews, and current sale pricing. Refreshed monthly.

body:
What actually matters in a phone under ₹25,000

The mid-range has changed completely in two years. A phone under ₹25,000 in 2026 gives you a 120Hz AMOLED, a 5,000mAh+ battery, 67W+ fast charging and a 50MP main camera with OIS — features that were flagship-exclusive in 2022. The risk is no longer bad hardware; it is choosing a model with poor software support, weak cooling, or a service network that does not cover your city.

For daily use, prioritise the chipset, display and battery before cameras. Snapdragon 7s Gen 2, Dimensity 8200, Dimensity 8300 and Exynos 1380 are the practical floor — they handle social media, BGMI, and on-device AI features without thermal throttling. AMOLED is non-negotiable at this price: LCD only appears in the cheapest sub-₹15,000 phones now.

Software support matters more than people realise. Samsung offers 4 years of OS + 5 years of security on the M35. OnePlus, Nothing and Realme offer 2-3 years. If you keep a phone for 3+ years, a Samsung Galaxy A or M, or a Pixel A-series, is the safer long-term bet even if its camera trails the Chinese competition at launch.

If you only buy one thing from this list: choose the OnePlus Nord CE 4 Lite 5G (8/256GB) when it dips under ₹23,000 on Amazon or OnePlus.in. Its 120Hz AMOLED, 5,500mAh battery and 80W SUPERVOOC charging cover the three things that matter most in a mid-range phone: smooth daily use, all-day battery, and a top-up that finishes in 30 minutes. Three years of OxygenOS updates are the closing argument.

The chipset cheat sheet

At ₹25,000, you will see Snapdragon 695, 6 Gen 1, 7s Gen 2, Dimensity 7050, 7300, 8200, 8300, and Exynos 1380. For everyday use all are fine, but the Dimensity 8300 and Snapdragon 7+ Gen 3 are the real performers — they approach last year's flagship Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 in benchmarks. If you game, prioritise cooling: phones with a stated vapour-chamber area over 3,500 mm² sustain performance longer.

AMOLED vs pOLED and why refresh rate is not everything

AMOLED and pOLED are both OLED; the difference is the substrate (rigid vs flexible) and pOLED allows slightly thinner bezels. Refresh rate (90Hz vs 120Hz vs 144Hz) is noticeable when scrolling but mostly indistinguishable in video. Peak brightness above 1,800 nits is what separates a phone you can read in direct sunlight from one you cannot. Touch sampling rate matters for gaming: 240Hz+ is the gaming-friendly spec.

Charging math that actually matters

67W charging takes a 5,000mAh battery from 0 to ~80% in 30 minutes, and 100% in roughly 45 minutes. 80W cuts another 5-7 minutes. Above 100W, gains flatten. What matters more: does the included charger reach those speeds, or do you need a separate PPS-compatible brick? Many phones now ship with a full-speed charger in the box, but verify before assuming.

Our top 5 picks

⭐ Top Pick

1. OnePlus Nord CE 4 Lite 5G (8/256GB)

Usually ₹22,000–₹24,500
ChipsetSnapdragon 695
Display6.67" 120Hz AMOLED
Battery5,500mAh + 80W
Camera50MP main with OIS
Updates3 yrs OxygenOS

The Nord CE 4 Lite is the easiest mid-range phone to recommend in 2026. The 120Hz AMOLED is bright enough for outdoor use, the 5,500mAh battery reliably lasts a full day of heavy use, and 80W SUPERVOOC charging takes the phone from 0 to 100% in under 45 minutes. OxygenOS 15 is clean, fast and free of heavy ads. The Snapdragon 695 is not the newest chip, but for social media, video, and casual gaming it remains more than capable.

Best for buyers who want a fuss-free, all-rounder with reliable software. The 256GB storage tier is the one to pick — it is usually only ₹1,500 more than 128GB and removes a real constraint three years from now.

✓ What works

  • Clean OxygenOS with three years of updates
  • 80W charging is class-leading in this range
  • 5,500mAh battery is genuinely all-day
  • AMOLED with good outdoor brightness
  • OIS on the main camera

✗ Trade-offs

  • Snapdragon 695 trails Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 in benchmarks
  • No telephoto camera (rare at this price)
  • Macro camera is mostly filler

🥈 Best Performance

2. Realme P3 Pro 5G (8/256GB)

Usually ₹21,000–₹24,000
ChipsetSnapdragon 7s Gen 2
Display6.7" 120Hz AMOLED
Battery5,500mAh + 67W
Camera50MP Sony IMX896 with OIS
BuildIP69 dust/water

The Realme P3 Pro is the most performance-focused phone in this list. Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 is roughly 40% faster than Snapdragon 695 in GPU-bound tests, and the phone holds high frame rates in BGMI and Genshin Impact for longer thanks to a substantial vapour-chamber cooler. The Sony IMX896 with OIS is one of the best main sensors in this segment, and Realme's colour science is more restrained than older Realme phones.

This is the right pick for gamers and heavy social media users. Realme UI 6.0 is heavier than OxygenOS, but it is fast and the bloatware is mostly removable.

✓ What works

  • Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 is the fastest chip in this bracket
  • IP69 rating — rare at this price
  • Strong sustained gaming performance
  • Sony IMX896 main camera with OIS
  • 67W charging is quick enough for daily use

✗ Trade-offs

  • Realme UI is heavier than OxygenOS / Hello UI
  • 2-3 years of OS updates only
  • Aggressive sale pricing makes timing hard
Check current price →

3. Motorola Edge 60 Fusion (8/256GB)

Usually ₹22,000–₹25,000
ChipsetDimensity 7300
Display6.67" 120Hz pOLED
Battery5,200mAh + 68W
Camera50MP main + 13MP ultrawide
SoftwareNear-stock Hello UI

Motorola's Edge 60 Fusion is the cleanest software experience in this list. Hello UI is close to stock Android with thoughtful additions (chop-chop flashlight, twist-for-camera, ready-for desktop) and almost no bloatware. The Dimensity 7300 is efficient — battery life comfortably reaches a day and a half of moderate use. The 13MP ultrawide is a real second camera, not a 2MP macro, and the ultrawide doubles as a competent macro shooter.

Pick this over OnePlus if clean Android and a useful ultrawide camera matter more than charging speed. Motorola's update commitment is shorter than Samsung but covers the practical lifetime of the phone.

✓ What works

  • Clean, near-stock Android experience
  • Useful ultrawide camera (not a 2MP macro)
  • IP68 rating on selected variants
  • Efficient Dimensity 7300 — strong battery life
  • 68W charging included in the box

✗ Trade-offs

  • 2 years of OS updates, 3 years of security
  • Camera processing trails OnePlus in low light
  • Moto service network is smaller than Samsung/OnePlus
Check current price →

4. Samsung Galaxy M35 5G (8/128GB)

Usually ₹19,500–₹22,000
ChipsetExynos 1380
Display6.6" 120Hz Super AMOLED
Battery6,000mAh + 25W
Camera50MP main with OIS
Updates4 yrs OS + 5 yrs security

The Galaxy M35 is the long-term value pick. Four years of OS updates and five years of security patches is unmatched in this bracket — it will receive Android 18 when it ships, while most competitors stop at Android 16. The 6,000mAh battery is the largest in this list and the phone easily lasts a day and a half. OneUI 7 is polished and Samsung Knox adds real security for users who keep sensitive data on their phone.

The trade-offs are real: 25W charging is slow next to OnePlus's 80W and Realme's 67W. The Exynos 1380 is also slightly behind Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 in gaming. If you charge overnight and rarely game, neither matters.

✓ What works

  • 4 yrs OS + 5 yrs security updates — class-leading
  • 6,000mAh battery is the largest here
  • OneUI 7 is well-optimised for daily use
  • Samsung Knox for security
  • Wider service network than competitors

✗ Trade-offs

  • 25W charging is slow by 2026 standards
  • Exynos 1380 trails Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 in gaming
  • Only 128GB at this price; 256GB costs more
Check current price →

5. Nothing CMF Phone 1 (8/128GB)

Usually ₹19,000–₹21,500
ChipsetDimensity 7300
Display6.67" 120Hz AMOLED
Battery5,000mAh + 33W
Camera50MP main + 2MP depth
BuildModular back, accessory point

The CMF Phone 1 is the most distinctive phone in this list, and the only one with a modular back, removable cover, and an accessory mounting point for a lanyard, kickstand or wallet. NothingOS 3.0 is among the cleanest Android skins available. The Dimensity 7300 is the same chip as the Motorola Edge 60 Fusion, with comparable daily performance. The 2MP depth camera is filler, but the main 50MP camera is competent in good light.

Pick it for the design and software. Skip it if you want the best camera or the fastest charging — the 33W brick is the slowest here.

✓ What works

  • Modular back with accessory ecosystem
  • Clean NothingOS with useful Glyph-style additions
  • Same Dimensity 7300 as the Edge 60 Fusion
  • Distinctive design — most unique in the list
  • Good value at the sub-₹21,000 sale price

✗ Trade-offs

  • 33W charging is slow
  • 2MP depth camera is filler
  • Smaller service network than Samsung
  • Software updates shorter than Samsung Galaxy M35

The one we recommend skipping

⚠️ Skip

Unbranded “flagship-killer” listings at ₹22,000 with no service network

ChipsetOften Helio G99
DisplayAMOLED 60-90Hz
Spec sheetMisleading
ServiceNone nearby
UpdatesOften abandoned in a year

Listings that advertise “12GB RAM + 256GB + 108MP” at ₹22,000 are almost always built on a Helio G99 or older Snapdragon 4-series chip, with a 60-90Hz panel, a weak 108MP sensor, and no authorised service network. Specifications are not experience: a Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 phone with 8GB of RAM and a 50MP Sony sensor will outperform a 12GB/108MP phone on a Helio G99 in every real-world test. The bigger numbers exist to rank in search results, not to make the phone better.

We also recommend skipping any phone whose brand has no authorised service in your city, no clear software update commitment, and no rating in the 80%+ user-reviews band on Amazon or Flipkart. A ₹3,000 saving is not worth a phone that becomes unsupported in 12 months.

The bottom line

Buy the OnePlus Nord CE 4 Lite when it lands near ₹22,000 with the 256GB storage. It is the easiest mid-range phone to live with for the next three years. Pick the Realme P3 Pro if gaming performance and IP69 are priorities. Choose the Samsung Galaxy M35 if you keep phones for 3+ years and value long software support above charging speed. The Motorola Edge 60 Fusion is the right call for clean Android, and the CMF Phone 1 wins on design and modular accessories.

Skip unbranded flagship-killer listings and 108MP Helio G99 phones with no service network. Spend a little more on a phone with documented software support and a real brand warranty in your city. The few thousand rupees saved is rarely worth the year of frustration when something goes wrong.

Frequently asked questions

Is a phone under ₹25,000 good enough for gaming?

Yes. Snapdragon 7s Gen 2, Dimensity 8200, Dimensity 8300 and Exynos 1380 chipsets handle BGMI, Genshin Impact and on-device AI features at medium-to-high settings. For sustained performance look for a vapour-chamber cooling system over 3,500 mm² and at least 8GB of RAM.

Should I get AMOLED or LCD in this range?

AMOLED is the practical default at ₹25,000. You get true blacks, better outdoor visibility on 1,800+ nit panels, and lower battery drain in dark mode. LCD only makes sense for the cheapest phones under ₹15,000.

How much RAM is enough?

8GB is the minimum in 2026, 12GB is comfortable for heavy multitasking. Storage: 128GB is the floor, 256GB is worth the premium if you shoot a lot of video. Many 256GB variants are only ₹1,500 more than 128GB.

Are mid-range phones good for photography?

Mid-range phones with a 50MP Sony IMX882/IMX896 or Samsung GN8 main sensor and OIS take genuinely good daylight and low-light photos. Telephoto is rare in this range; expect a competent 2MP macro that you will rarely use.

How long will software updates last?

Samsung offers 4 years of OS + 5 years of security on the M35. OnePlus, Nothing, Motorola and Realme offer 2-3 years. If long-term updates matter, Samsung and Pixel A-series are the safer picks.
